clue.text: One who's got to join metal parts outside bistro?

definitions.text: One who's got to join metal parts outside bistro?

indicators.note: outside says the word for joining metal goes around the word for the eatery

parts.note: to solder is to join metal pieces with molten alloy
a caff is British slang for a cheap cafe, a humble bistro

explanation.surface: A metalworker is needed to weld something together outside a little restaurant.
explanation.walkthrough: CAFF is British slang for a cheap cafe. The whole clue also describes the worker who clamps metal poles together outside a building such as a bistro.
explanation.definitionFit: This worker erects the temporary framework of clamped metal poles put up around buildings under repair.

clue.text: Unpopular person with Union Jack being led by special constable

indicators.note: being led by puts the special constable's letters in front of the sailor's

parts.note: SC is the abbreviation for a special constable, a volunteer police officer
a jack is a sailor, and AB (able seaman) is the usual crossword sailor

explanation.surface: Someone disliked, carrying a Union Jack, is escorted by a volunteer policeman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Union Jack' looks like the flag, but the phrase splits: 'Union' ends the definition and 'Jack' is the sailor AB.
explanation.definitionFit: A strikebreaker who works on during a strike is hated by the trade union and its members.

clue.text: Hazel maybe tailed lunatic going round about

indicators.note: going round says the shortened word surrounds the word for about
tailed means the final letter of the word for a madman is docked

parts.note: a nutter is British slang for a lunatic
re is Latin-derived for about, concerning

explanation.surface: A madman with a tail is circling around something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tailed' docks the last letter, leaving NUTTE, which then wraps around the word for about.
explanation.definitionFit: The hazel bears cobnuts and filberts, so it is an example of a nut-bearing tree.

clue.text: Not for profit, in a way

indicators.note: in says the word for profit sits inside the article plus the road abbreviation

parts.note: ST, short for street, is a way
gain means profit

explanation.surface: A charity runs not for profit, in its own manner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not for profit' reads as the charity phrase, but the definition is just 'Not for', and 'profit' joins the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Being opposed to something is the opposite of being in favour of it.

clue.text: Holy man had us excited

indicators.note: excited suggests the letters of had us are stirred up into a new order

explanation.surface: A religious ascetic found the two of us thrilling.
explanation.definitionFit: In Hinduism this is a wandering ascetic or sage who has renounced worldly life.

clue.text: Article pinched? Description of thieves perhaps unreasonable

parts.note: a is the indefinite article
bit, the past tense of bite, means nipped or pinched
thieves are proverbially described as thick, in the phrase thick as thieves

explanation.surface: A newspaper article about stolen goods, describing the robbers, seems rather unfair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'thick as thieves' means very close friends, so 'thick' describes thieves.
explanation.definitionFit: The British idiom for behaviour that is a little unfair or too much to accept.

clue.text: One mum not so friendly?

parts.note: mum means silent, so one who is not mum is talking, and the phrase so friendly describes people still civil to each other

explanation.surface: A mother who is not very warm towards others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mum' looks like a mother but means silent: someone not mum is talking, and so on friendly enough terms to do so.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes people who are civil enough to talk to each other, though perhaps not close friends.

clue.text: Chance of us mums somehow catching husband more or less equal

indicators.note: catching says the rearranged letters take in the abbreviation for husband
somehow signals that the letters of chance of us mums are to be rearranged in some fashion

explanation.surface: Mothers taking a gamble on catching a husband stand roughly level.
explanation.walkthrough: 'somehow' rearranges CHANCEOFUSMUMS and 'catching' puts H into the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase, from a Victorian play, means things so alike there is little to choose between them.

clue.text: Gracious kind regularly getting personal and familiar

parts.note: well is an exclamation of surprise, like gracious

indicators.note: regularly takes every other letter of kind, the first and third

parts.note: own means personal, belonging to oneself

explanation.surface: A gracious, kindly person who regularly becomes personal and friendly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gracious' reads as polite but is the exclamation WELL; 'regularly' gives KN from kind.
explanation.definitionFit: Something widely known to everyone is familiar to the public.

clue.text: Sheet of rock, dropped off when cut at the end

indicators.note: cut at the end means the final letter of the word for dozed is removed

parts.note: napped means dropped off, fell asleep briefly

explanation.surface: A slab of stone fell away once its far end was cut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dropped off' looks like falling, but it is dozing: NAPPED, cut to lose its final D.
explanation.definitionFit: In geology this is a large body of rock folded and pushed far over the underlying strata.

clue.text: Burglar's awful fate after pinching beer

indicators.note: pinching says the rearranged letters take in the word for beer
awful indicates the letters of fate are made into a bad, jumbled version

parts.note: ale is a kind of beer

explanation.surface: A burglar faces a terrible end after stealing some beer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'awful' rearranges the letters to TEAF before the beer goes in. TEA LEAF is Cockney rhyming slang for thief.
explanation.definitionFit: Cockney rhyming slang: the phrase rhymes with thief, so it names a thief or burglar.

clue.text: Was Number One dropped when heard on radio?

indicators.note: heard on radio signals the word is to be judged by its sound alone

parts.note: rained means came down in drops

explanation.surface: A song was top of the charts but fell when it was heard on the radio.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number One' suggests a hit record, but it means the monarch: one who ruled.
explanation.definitionFit: A monarch who ruled was the top person in the land.

clue.text: Better no longer to have a Liberal's mind

indicators.note: no longer to have means the letters for a and Liberal are taken out

parts.note: healed means made better, cured
A plus L, the abbreviation for Liberal

explanation.surface: It is better that a Liberal should be gone from someone's mind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Better' looks like an adjective but is a verb, 'made better', HEALED; removing A and L leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To mind something is to pay attention to it or take notice.

clue.text: Kind fellow responsible for this puzzle — ex-Times employee?

parts.note: type means kind or sort
a setter is the person who compiles a crossword

explanation.surface: A kind compiler of this crossword, who once worked for the newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: Newspapers once employed compositors to arrange metal type by hand; computer setting ended the job.
explanation.definitionFit: This compositor arranged printing type, a newspaper job now largely gone.

clue.text: Howler affecting visibility in a way in hospital bedroom

parts.note: san is short for sanatorium, a hospital

indicators.note: in says the abbreviation for a road goes inside the shared sleeping room

parts.note: dorm is short for dormitory, a bedroom
ST is short for street, a way

explanation.surface: A howling wind cuts visibility in the hospital ward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Howler' suggests a blunder, but it is a howling storm.
explanation.definitionFit: A desert storm blowing grit through the air howls and blots out the view.

clue.text: Did something demanded after departure of old partner

indicators.note: after departure of means the letters for a former partner are removed

parts.note: exacted means demanded
an ex is a former partner

explanation.surface: Something was demanded once a former partner had left.
explanation.definitionFit: To have acted is to have taken action, performed a deed.

clue.text: Biscuit with something in it killing, perhaps, doctor? That is!

parts.note: making a killing means earning a fortune
to cook means to doctor, falsify accounts

explanation.surface: A biscuit that hides a deadly poison: was the doctor responsible?
explanation.walkthrough: 'killing' suggests murder but is a large profit; 'doctor' is the verb, to falsify, as in cooking the books.
explanation.definitionFit: A crisp folded biscuit served in Chinese restaurants holds a slip of paper with a prediction inside.

clue.text: Rest respond to storyteller in kind?

definitions.meaning: storyteller means a liar, and responding in kind means telling a lie in return

explanation.surface: Relax, and answer a narrator with a tale of your own.
explanation.definitionFit: Reclining to relax is one sense; the other is literal, telling a falsehood in return to someone who fibs.

clue.text: Girl's over the moon, with new fencing

indicators.note: over in a down clue means the girl's name stands above the moon's

parts.note: Eva's, a girl's name with possessive
Io is a moon of Jupiter

explanation.surface: A girl is delighted with her newly built fence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over the moon' reads as delighted, but 'over' places EVAS above IO, a moon of Jupiter; 'fencing' is verbal dodging.
explanation.definitionFit: Verbal sparring that parries questions without answering is dodging, avoidance of the issue.

clue.text: Caretaker recceing old ruins

indicators.note: ruins means the letters of recceing and the old abbreviation are wrecked and rebuilt

explanation.surface: A caretaker scouting out ancient ruins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ruins' looks like a noun for remains, but it is a verb, wrecking the letters of RECCEING plus O.
explanation.definitionFit: A doorkeeper or porter of a block of flats who looks after the building.

clue.text: Design method for which graduate brought up equipment

parts.note: BA, Bachelor of Arts, is a graduate

indicators.note: brought up in a down clue means the word for gear is read from bottom to top

parts.note: kit means equipment

explanation.surface: A design technique for which a graduate brought up some gear.
explanation.definitionFit: A way of patterning cloth by waxing areas so they resist the dye.

clue.text: Like little chap, home bird, to make prompt repair

parts.note: as means like
titch is British slang for a small person
in means at home
bird is British slang for a prison sentence, time

explanation.surface: Like a small boy at home with a pet bird, ready to fix things promptly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bird' is British rhyming slang (birdlime = time) for prison time; TITCH is a British word for a small person.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb says sewing a tear early saves nine later, so it stands for a timely fix.

clue.text: Old farm tool welcome when working well? On the contrary!

definitions.text: when working well? On the contrary!

parts.note: a sickle is a curved blade once used for reaping
ave is Latin for hail, a greeting or welcome

explanation.surface: An antique farm implement is welcome when it still works well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the contrary' turns the definition around: this is time off when someone is not well enough to work.
explanation.definitionFit: This is paid time off granted to an employee who is ill, so not fit for the job.

clue.text: American appearing in English poet's band

indicators.note: appearing in says the abbreviation for American goes inside the poet's name

parts.note: Stephen Spender was an English poet

explanation.surface: An American shows up in an English poet's group of musicians.
explanation.walkthrough: 'band' looks like a music group, but it is a strap. Spender, not Spenser, is the poet needed.
explanation.definitionFit: A garter or elastic strap that holds up a stocking or sock.

clue.text: A wing containing the smallest room, in a way cold

parts.note: the smallest room is a jokey name for the toilet, the loo
a fly is a flap or wing, as a fly on a tent or the flies of a theatre

explanation.surface: A building wing has a toilet that is, in a way, chilly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the smallest room' is a British euphemism for the toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting distantly and without warmth is a manner that is cool and reserved.

clue.text: Rattle coming from machine-gunner — verifiably

indicators.note: coming from says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A soldier with a machine gun can be shown to be shaken.
explanation.definitionFit: To rattle someone is to upset their composure and nerve.

clue.text: Trade bans succeeded, hexing one

indicators.note: bans means the abbreviation for succeeded is excluded from the word for trade

parts.note: to switch is to trade or swap

explanation.surface: Trade restrictions worked, putting a curse on someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bans' looks like a noun in 'Trade bans', but it is a verb: SWITCH bans S.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman casting spells and curses is a sorceress.

clue.text: Winemaker turning to a little Scotch?

indicators.note: turning means the words for to and a little Scotch are read backwards together

parts.note: a nip is a small measure of spirits

explanation.surface: A winemaker switches to a small whisky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turning' reverses TO plus NIP, the whole run read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A grape variety, as in Pinot Noir, from which wine is made.
